\chapter{The Thing Said}
\label{ch:ml-ennu}
\hlchaptermodality{72}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can report what somebody said, thought, knew or asked, by putting the quotative ennu after a sentence I can already say.}

From cold: the marker that turns any sentence into the thing said, and the four verbs it can hand that sentence to — with nothing inside the quoted sentence rebuilt.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ennŭ]{\ml{എന്ന്} (ennŭ) — the word that makes a sentence quotable}

\label{lesson:ML-C72-ennu}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{enikkŭ malayāḷaṁ aṟiyāṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}I know Malayalam.\textquotedblright{} A whole sentence, and yours since the knowing chapter.

Now say \emph{ñān paṟayunnu}. Today one word joins those two.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്ന്}} — \emph{ennŭ} — \textbf{marks the sentence before it as the thing said}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം}\textquotedblright{} \ml{എന്ന്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പറയുന്നു}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textquotedblleft{}enikkŭ malayāḷaṁ aṟiyāṁ\textquotedblright{} ennŭ ñān paṟayunnu} — 'I say, \textquotedblleft{}I know Malayalam.\textquotedblright{}'
\end{quote}

\textbf{Nothing in the quoted sentence changed.} It is the same five syllables you have been saying since chapter nine, sitting in front of \emph{ennŭ} exactly as they stand on their own.

That is the whole of it, and it is worth more than the one word costs. English rebuilds a reported sentence — \emph{I know Malayalam} becomes \emph{that I know Malayalam}, and a different person or tense forces more changes still. \textbf{Malayalam leaves the sentence alone and puts a marker after it.}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where it sits}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
the sentence said & \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം}} \\
the marker & \textbf{\ml{എന്ന്}} \\
who says it & \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പറയുന്നു}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the three rows in that order and you have the sentence. \textbf{The quoted part comes first and the saying comes last}, which is the opposite of English and the same order Malayalam uses everywhere else — the verb at the end.

You have seen this shape before without the marker: \textbf{\ml{എന്നാൽ}} (\emph{ennāl}), the word for \emph{but}, begins with the same \textbf{\ml{എന്ന}}. They are relatives, and meeting one helps you notice the other on a page.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{enikkŭ malayāḷaṁ aṟiyāṁ}
  \item the same thing again with \emph{ennŭ ñān paṟayunnu} after it
  \item which of the two parts came out unchanged
  \item where the saying-verb sits, and where English would put it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ml{എന്ന്}} do? (\textbf{Marks the sentence in front of it as the thing said}.) What has to change inside that sentence? (\textbf{Nothing}.) Which comes first, the saying or the thing said? (\textbf{The thing said} — the verb goes last.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ennŭ cintikkunnu]{\ml{എന്ന്} \ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു} — the marker does not care which verb follows}

\label{lesson:ML-C72-ennu-more}



\begin{quote}
Say your quoted sentence with \emph{ennŭ ñān paṟayunnu} after it.

Now swap the last verb for a different one. That is today's whole lesson.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one marker, four verbs}]
\textbf{\ml{എന്ന്}} marks the thing said. What happens to it afterwards is up to the verb at the end, and you already have four of them:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the verb after it} & \textbf{what the sentence becomes} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{പറയുന്നു}} \emph{paṟayunnu} & I \textbf{say} it \\
\textbf{\ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു}} \emph{cintikkunnu} & I \textbf{think} it \\
\textbf{\ml{അറിയാം}} \emph{aṟiyāṁ} & I \textbf{know} it \\
\textbf{\ml{ചോദിക്കുന്നു}} \emph{cōdikkunnu} & I \textbf{ask} it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം}\textquotedblright{} \ml{എന്ന്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{\textquotedblleft{}enikkŭ malayāḷaṁ aṟiyāṁ\textquotedblright{} ennŭ ñān cintikkunnu} — 'I think I know Malayalam.'
\end{quote}

\textbf{This is why the marker is worth a chapter.} It is one word, and it turns every sentence you can already build into something you can report, wonder about, claim to know, or put as a question — without learning a new shape for any of them.

The knowing verb keeps its own shape: \textbf{\ml{അറിയാം}} puts what is known at the front and leaves the knower in the dative, so the sentence arrives at you rather than being done by you. The marker sits in front of it unchanged.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the quoted sentence, then \emph{ennŭ ñān paṟayunnu}
  \item the same, then \emph{ennŭ ñān cintikkunnu}
  \item which part of the sentence you changed each time, and which part you did not
  \item the four verbs the marker can hand a sentence to
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does \textbf{\ml{എന്ന്}} change when the verb after it changes? (\textbf{No}.) Name two verbs it can hand a sentence to. (\emph{\textbf{Paṟayunnu}}, \emph{\textbf{cintikkunnu}} — also \emph{aṟiyāṁ} and \emph{cōdikkunnu}.) And how much of the quoted sentence has to be rebuilt? (\textbf{None of it}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paṟaññatŭ]{(the thing said) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R72-ennu-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{I say} in Malayalam, and say which three places in this book used that verb before anybody taught it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three pieces, in this order}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
a sentence you can already say & \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{അറിയാം}} \\
the marker & \textbf{\ml{എന്ന്}} \\
what happens to it & \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പറയുന്നു}} / \textbf{\ml{ചിന്തിക്കുന്നു}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The middle row never changes and the top row never changes.} Only the bottom one does, and it picks between verbs you have had since the thirties.

That is the payoff worth holding on to: \textbf{every sentence in this book is now something you can report}. The chapter added one marker and one verb, and what it bought was the whole of what you already knew, usable a second way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three rows in order, as one sentence
  \item it again with the thinking verb at the end
  \item what English would have to change that Malayalam leaves alone
  \item the four verbs that can stand in the bottom row
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the marker? (\textbf{\ml{എന്ന്}}.) What does it do to the sentence in front of it? (\textbf{Nothing} — it marks it as the thing said and leaves it whole.) Where does the saying-verb go? (\textbf{Last}.) And what is \emph{to say}? (\emph{\textbf{Paṟayuka}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
